define-a-useful-request.title: What does “help me order dinner” mean?

sections.title: Start with a tired, hungry person
sections.content:
It is 7:30 p.m. You want something spicy for under $25, including fees. The assistant returns twenty restaurant names. That is information, but you still have to do the comparison yourself. Your product should help someone reach a suitable decision with less effort.

This module is the first step toward a DoorDash ordering assistant. You will build the request-understanding stage. The examples use fictional information; recommendations and ordering come later.

First separate a hard constraint (a requirement), a preference (something to optimize), and an unknown (something to ask about or verify). “Must be under $25 total” is a constraint. “Thai would be nice” is a preference. An unstated delivery area is unknown.

sections.alt: A diner’s request branches into a wallet and receipt representing the $25 total constraint, a Thai noodle bowl representing a preference, and a map with a question mark representing the unknown delivery area.
sections.caption: Separate what must hold, what would be nice, and what is missing.

sections.question: Match each part of the request to its role.

pairs.left: Must cost less than $25 including fees

sections.explanation: Constraints define acceptable results; preferences rank them; unknowns require clarification or reliable information.

sections.title: A price is only useful if you know what it includes
sections.content:
A fictional meal costs $19. Delivery is $3, service fees are $2, and tax is $2. The total is already $26 before a tip. The menu price alone cannot establish that the order fits a $25 all-in budget.

Do not guess missing fees. Show which prices are known and which remain unverified. If a user says “under $25,” ask whether that includes fees, tax, and any tip rather than silently choosing an interpretation.

sections.question: Which response best handles a $25 all-in limit when delivery fees are unknown?

options.text: This $23 meal is definitely within budget.
The meal is $23; I need the remaining charges before confirming the total.
Choose the cheapest photo on the menu.

sections.explanation: Only the second response preserves the constraint without inventing a total. A cheap menu item can still lead to an over-budget order.

sections.title: Define success before adding features
sections.content:
For this first module, measure request fidelity: did we preserve the stated requirements? Also check unsupported assumptions: did we invent a location, currency, or preference? Finally inspect question usefulness: did the follow-up remove a real obstacle?

A small test set is enough to begin: write five fictional requests and expected summaries. Count correct fields and invented fields. Later, you can measure time to a suitable decision with real users. A short interaction is useful only if it still respects their needs.

sections.question: Name two ways to judge whether the request-understanding step helped the user.
sections.sample_answer: Check that the summary preserves the all-in budget and that the next question resolves a missing detail instead of asking something already answered.
sections.explanation: Measure behavior tied to the task. Message count or enthusiastic wording alone does not show success.

understand-model-context.title: What the model knows—and what it needs

sections.title: A confident answer is not a receipt
sections.content:
Imagine the assistant says, “Delivery is $2 and the restaurant is open.” Before trusting it, ask: where did those facts come from? If neither you nor a connected source supplied them, the response has not established they are current.

A large language model (LLM) learns patterns during training and generates responses from its available context. It can interpret “Thai would be nice” as a preference. That capability does not itself provide current restaurant availability.

Keep three things separate: instructions describe the task, user input describes the request, and external evidence supplies facts such as a current menu.

sections.alt: Instructions and user input enter the model. External menu information must be supplied through a separate source; a response alone does not verify availability.
sections.caption: Trace each claim back to the information that supports it.

sections.statement: A confident delivery estimate proves the assistant checked a live source.
sections.explanation: Confidence is a property of the wording. Verification requires evidence from an appropriate source.

sections.title: Tokens are pieces; context is the working space
sections.content:
Models process text as tokens, which may be whole words, parts of words, or punctuation. A token is not always a word. The context window limits the information processed in a request; the exact accounting depends on the model.

Think of context as the material available on a desk. The current request, relevant prior messages, instructions, and tool results may all occupy space. A long conversation does not guarantee that every earlier message remains available.

When shortening a dinner conversation, preserve active requirements and corrections. Keep “vegetarian” and “$25 including fees”; remove irrelevant small talk first. Summaries can also make mistakes, so inspect them. See Anthropic’s context-window documentation for a provider example.

sections.question: Which information should survive when you shorten the conversation?

options.text: All greetings, even if the budget is lost.
The current dietary requirements, budget, and corrections.
Only the most recent restaurant name.

sections.explanation: Preserve the facts that determine an acceptable result. The latest message may be a correction that relies on earlier requirements.

sections.title: Tools provide a connection to the outside
sections.content:
An API is a defined way for software to request information or an action from other software. A tool makes a capability available to an assistant. The application must execute and check a tool request; naming a tool in a prompt does not connect it.

A future menu tool could supply prices and timestamps. For this module, label all restaurant examples as fictional. Do not claim that a working DoorDash integration exists.

This is a workflow: the application follows a defined sequence. We can add agent-directed choices when the problem needs them. This distinction follows Anthropic’s foundational workflow guidance.

sections.question: Match the information to its appropriate source.
sections.explanation: User preferences, operational rules, and current external facts have different origins. Keep those origins visible.

flashcards.front: Does an LLM inherently know a live delivery charge?
flashcards.back: No. Current charges require an appropriate current source.
It defines how software requests information or actions from other software.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes a workflow from an agent-directed process?
flashcards.back: A workflow follows predefined paths; an agent can choose its next steps dynamically.

structure-the-request.title: Turn a conversation into usable fields

sections.title: Give the application a labeled form
sections.content:
Humans understand many ways of saying the same thing. Software benefits from consistent field names and types. JSON is a text format for labeled values, like a form the application can read.

In JSON, text uses quotation marks, numbers do not, true and false represent yes and no, and null means a deliberately empty value. A list uses square brackets.

For “Something spicy under $25 including fees; Thai would be nice,” this is a possible structured interpretation. Currency and dietary restrictions remain unknown:

{
  "cuisine_preferences": [
    "Thai"
  ],
  "spice_preference": "spicy",
  "budget_amount": 25,
  "currency": null,
  "includes_fees": true,
  "dietary_restrictions": null,
  "delivery_area": null
}

sections.alt: The phrase Thai would be nice maps to cuisine preferences. Under $25 maps to budget amount. Unstated dietary restrictions map to null.
sections.caption: A structured response preserves evidence; it does not create missing facts.

sections.question: Match each request detail to its field.
sections.explanation: Consistent fields let the application compare and display values without interpreting a different prose format every time.

sections.title: Unknown is different from none
sections.content:
If the user has not mentioned dietary restrictions, use null. If they explicitly say “I have no dietary restrictions,” an empty list can represent that answer in our format. These states mean different things.

Keep inference modest. A dollar sign alone does not tell us which dollar currency is intended. Nor does a preferred cuisine establish someone’s location. Ask when an unknown becomes necessary for the task.

sections.question: The user never mentions dietary restrictions. What should our field contain?

options.text: An empty list, because silence means none.
null, because the information is unknown.
Vegetarian, because it is a reasonable default.

sections.explanation: null preserves missing information. An empty list would assert that no restrictions exist, which the user has not said.

sections.title: Write a prompt the model can follow
sections.content:
A useful prompt states the task, input, rules, and output format. For example: “Extract dinner preferences from the supplied request. Preserve explicit requirements. Use null for unknown values. Return these seven fields as JSON. Do not recommend a restaurant or invent fees.”

Include a worked input and output if it helps explain the task. Keep instructions separate from the user’s request so quoted restaurant text does not silently become an application rule.

A schema defines expected fields and types. Provider structured-output features can constrain format, but your application must still check whether values make sense and match the request. See Google’s structured-output guidance.

sections.question: Improve this instruction: “Fill in all dinner preferences, guessing anything missing.”
sections.sample_answer: Extract only supported preferences. Use null for unstated details, preserve the budget’s meaning, and return the agreed JSON fields.
sections.explanation: A clear output contract helps software, while explicit unknowns protect the meaning of the user’s request.

build-the-conversation-loop.title: Build, inspect, and improve the first loop

sections.title: Choose the next useful question
sections.content:
Once you have a draft summary, ask what blocks the next step. If the delivery area is missing, ask for an area before pretending to compare local restaurants. If the user has already supplied it, avoid asking again.

Use a small sequence: read → extract → validate → clarify → update. A correction updates the relevant field while preserving earlier requirements. “Actually vegetarian” should not erase the budget.

Open the Dinner Request Lab beside this lesson. It uses explicitly labeled sample responses, so you can inspect the workflow without an API key. It does not call a model or place an order.

sections.alt: Five steps: read the request, extract fields, validate structure, clarify missing details, and update the summary.
sections.caption: This first workflow makes each step visible before live tools are added.

sections.question: The user gave their budget and dietary needs but no delivery area. What should come next?

options.text: Ask the same budget question again.
Ask which area they want delivery to.
Claim a nearby restaurant delivers to them.

sections.explanation: Ask for an unresolved detail that matters to the next step. Do not invent location or repeat answered questions.

sections.title: Check structure and meaning separately
sections.content:
The lab has an editable JSON box. Delete a comma and validate: the application should explain that the format cannot be read. Restore it, then change the budget to 250. The format may pass even though the meaning is wrong for a $25 request.

This is the difference between structural validation and semantic checking. Structural checks catch missing fields or wrong types. Comparing the output with the original request catches a well-formed but incorrect interpretation.

An honest recovery message explains what failed and gives the user a way to retry. Avoid showing a stale “success” summary after the current response fails validation.

sections.statement: Valid JSON guarantees that the assistant correctly understood the user’s budget.
sections.explanation: A value can have the correct type and still be wrong. The number 250 is valid JSON but contradicts a $25 request.

sections.title: Make one change and observe the result
sections.content:
In the lab, load the worked example, validate it, and read the suggested clarification. Enter a fictional area using the follow-up field and update the summary. Then load the vegetarian correction case and confirm the $25 budget survives.

For the guided build, save the lab page to your computer and open its source in a text editor. HTML defines the page; CSS styles it; JavaScript supplies behavior. Search for nextQuestion. Change the wording of the delivery-area question, save, and refresh. The question should change without altering the budget.

Keep a baseline before using AI-assisted coding. Ask your coding assistant: “Explain nextQuestion line by line, then change only its delivery-area wording. Preserve the rest of the behavior and show me how to verify it.” Inspect the change yourself.

Extra model calls can add waiting time and cost. Begin with the smallest working loop and measure it before adding more steps. In this local simulation, the displayed validation duration is browser processing time, not model latency. A live extraction model and DoorDash connection are later course milestones.

sections.question: What should happen when the extraction response cannot be parsed?
sections.sample_answer: Hide the invalid summary, explain that the response format could not be read, retain the editable input, and offer a repair or retry path.
key_points: Do not present invalid output as success
sections.explanation: Good recovery preserves user effort and makes the current state clear.
